draft.title: Unconventional monetary policy
card: Normally the RBA steers the economy by moving the cash rate. In 2020 the cash rate was cut to a record low of 0.1%, close to zero, so it could not be cut much further.
The RBA bought government bonds from the market. This pushed down longer-term interest rates, such as the rate on a fixed-rate loan, which the cash rate does not reach directly.
The RBA lent money to banks at very low rates for a set period. This kept the banks' costs low, so they could keep lending to households and businesses at low rates.
These tools are called unconventional because they went beyond moving the cash rate. Their aim was the same: to support spending and jobs while keeping interest rates low.
draft.remember: When the cash rate cannot fall further, the RBA can buy bonds and fund banks cheaply to keep rates low.

a.q: Why did the RBA use bond purchases and cheap funding for banks in 2020 and 2021?
opts: The cash rate was near zero, so it had little room to fall
The cash rate was high, so it needed to be raised further
Inflation was far above target, so it needed to be cut
The government wanted to raise income tax to pay for bonds
a.why: With the cash rate near zero, cutting it further was not an option, so the RBA used other tools to keep interest rates low. The tempting idea that it was fighting high inflation is wrong, because these tools kept rates low to support spending.
a.clue: Think about how much room the cash rate had left to fall.

b.q: In 2021 the RBA buys government bonds in the market. What is the main effect it is aiming for?
opts: Lower longer-term interest rates, such as fixed loan rates
Higher longer-term interest rates, such as fixed loan rates
A higher cash rate, to slow spending in the economy
Lower government spending, to cut the budget deficit
b.why: Buying bonds pushes down longer-term rates, which makes borrowing cheaper and supports spending. A higher cash rate is the wrong answer: the tool is used because the cash rate is already near zero and the aim is to keep rates low.
b.clue: The aim was to keep borrowing costs low, not raise them.

a.best: The cash rate was near zero, so it had little room to fall

b.best: Lower longer-term interest rates, such as fixed loan rates
